A clamor arose throughout the entire city,
A disturbance in the imagination of that Sultan.
The hearts of the city's elite and commoners were lost,
Wondering what distress and calamity had occurred.
Is a conquering enemy intending to attack us?
Or has a celestial plague arisen from the Unseen?
For Dalqak has arrived in a rough, tattered cloak,
Having killed several swift horses along the road.
The people gathered at the King’s palace,
Asking why he arrived with such frantic haste.
From his speed, a foul exertion was evident;
A roar and agitation filled the city of Termez.
One person raised both hands in prayer,
While another, out of dread, cried out in woe.
From the outcry, the sedition, the fear, and the punishment,
Every heart was swept away by a hundred kinds of fancies.
Everyone made a prediction based on their own conjecture,
Wondering what fire had fallen into the wool.
The King quickly sought a path and gave him entry;
When he kissed the ground, the King said: "Hey, what happened?"
To anyone who asked of his condition in that bitterness,
He would place a finger to his lips, saying: "Hush!"
This behavior of his inflamed the King's imagination;
Everyone became stunned and paralyzed by the agitation.
Dalqak gestured: "O Munificent King,
Grant me a moment so that I may catch my breath,
Until my fleeting intellect returns to me,
For I have fallen into a wondrous world."
After an hour, during which the King’s throat and mouth
Grew bitter from the suspicion of his thoughts—
For he had never seen Dalqak in such a state,
As there was no companion more pleasant than him.
He used to always practice trickery and jesting;
He kept the King joyful and laughing.
He would make him laugh so much in his seat
That the King would clutch his belly, doubled over,
Until his body would break into a sweat from the force of laughter,
Falling forward from the intensity of his mirth.
Yet today, he is thus pale and bitter,
Placing a finger to his lips, saying: "O King, be silent!"
Imagination upon imagination, fancy upon fancy;
The King wondered what punishment would come upon him.
For the King’s heart was filled with grief and caution,
Because the Khwarazm-Shah was a great shedder of blood.
He had killed many kings of that region,
Either by guile or by the power of that stubborn one.
The King of Termez was trembling in his suspicion,
And Dalqak’s performance only increased that dread.
The King said: "Speak quickly, what is the situation?
From whom is this turmoil and agitation of yours?"
He replied: "I heard in the village that the King
Has issued a proclamation at every crossroads,
Saying: 'I want someone who, in three days,
Can reach Samarkand,' and if he is still successful,
'I have set aside treasures for him in exchange.'
When the purpose is achieved through the message,
I hurried to him for that reason,
To say that I do not have that ability!
Such a lowly task does not suit one like me;
Do not weave the thread of this hope upon me."

# The Nahid Maqama

Isa ibn Hisham narrated to us, saying:
I turned with a group of my companions to the courtyard of a tent seeking hospitality from its people. A man with a parched complexion came out to us and said: "Who are you?" We said: "Guests who have not tasted an enemy <note>idiom for food</note> for three days." He said: "Move aside." Then he said: "O youths, what do you think of a portion of <term>nahida</term> <gloss>a dish of butter and flour</gloss> as white as a bald man's pate, in a wide bowl, crowned with the froth of a great camel's hump, one portion of which fills the mouth? It is for a group of hungry, thirsty men on their fifth day without water. The tooth disappears into it, and its date-stones are like the tongues of birds. They gulp down the <term>nahida</term> with bowls of milk they have milked from old, sturdy camels. Do you desire it, O youths?" We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" The old man guffawed and said: "And your uncle <note>referring to himself</note> also desires it!"

Then he said: "What is your opinion, O youths, of fine white bread like pieces of silver ingots, arranged on a leather mat smelling of mimosa bark? A bright, clever, and nimble youth leaps to it, kneading it without shaking or rattling it. He makes it softer than a gentle king, then moistens it with milk or a heavy pestle. Then he turns to it, twists it, and leaves it in the corner of the oven until it rises without being overbaked. Then he goes to the wood of the <term>ghada</term> tree and lights the fire. When its flame dies down, he prepares its bed of hot ashes, then takes his dough and throws it in after perfecting its color. He spreads it out, covers it, and when it is cooked and ready, he heaps upon it hot stones until the two heats meet. When he covers them on the matching embers with a lid, and it splits open clearly, its crust resembling thin layers, and its redness like the red of the famous Hijazi dates known as 'Mother of Locusts' or 'Ibn Tab's cluster,' he pours over it white honey like snow until it sinks into the fats, and the heart of the bread drinks what is upon it. I present it to you and you swallow it in great gulps. Do you desire it, O youths?"

He said: Each of us craned our necks at his description, our mouths watered, and we smacked our lips. We said: "Yes, by God, we desire it!" parts out of one hundred and nine parts of a share. You set the share as one hundred and nine parts, then multiply thirteen by one hundred and nine parts and add eighty parts to that. This results in one thousand four hundred and ninety-seven, and the husband's portion is three hundred and twenty-seven.

If a woman leaves two sisters and a husband <note>The Arabic text mentions a wife, but the context of the division suggests a husband or a specific legal distribution</note>, and she bequeaths to a man the equivalent of a sister's portion minus one-eighth of what remains of the estate after the legacy. The calculation for this is to establish the legal shares <term>al-faridah</term> <gloss>the prescribed inheritance portions</gloss> from twelve shares, where each sister receives one-third of what remains of the estate after the legacy. This is the estate minus the legacy. You know that one-eighth of what remains plus the legacy equals a sister's portion. Thus, one-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy. Therefore, one-eighth of the estate minus one-eighth of the legacy plus the legacy equals a sister's portion, which is one-eighth of the estate and seven-eighths of the legacy. The entire estate then equals three-eighths of the estate plus three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. Subtract three-eighths of the estate from the whole estate, leaving five-eighths of the estate equaling three legacies and five-eighths of a legacy. The entire estate then equals five legacies and four-fifths of a legacy. Thus, the estate is twenty-nine, the legacy is five, and the portion is eight.

In another type of legacy: a man dies and leaves four sons, and bequeaths to one man the equivalent of one of his sons' portions, and to another man one-quarter of what remains of the third. Know that the legacy is only taken from the third.

Just as an ignorant judge who is unfamiliar with the <term>Sunnah</term> <gloss>the traditions and practices of the Prophet</gloss> is not excused if he errs in a ruling, so too the one who judges concerning existing things is not excused if the conditions for judgment are not found in him. Rather, he is either a sinner or an infidel. If it is required of a judge in matters of the permitted and the forbidden that the means of <term>ijtihad</term> <gloss>independent legal reasoning</gloss> be gathered in him—which is the knowledge of the <term>usul</term> <gloss>fundamentals or principles</gloss> and the knowledge of <term>istinbat</term> <gloss>deduction or inference</gloss> from those principles by <term>qiyas</term> <gloss>analogy</gloss>—how much more so should this be required for the one who judges existing things? I mean that he must know the rational first principles and the method of deduction from them.

In short, error regarding the Law is of two kinds. Either it is an error for which the person who is qualified to investigate that matter is excused—just as a skilled physician is excused if he errs in the art of medicine, and a skilled judge is excused if he errs in a ruling, while the one who is not of that standing is not excused—or it is an error for which no one among people is excused. Its Sultan is King Badr al-Din ibn Qaraman <note>the name is pronounced with a short 'a' sound on the Qaf and the Ra</note>. Before him, it belonged to Ashqiya Musa, who surrendered it to King al-Nasir <note>the Mamluk Sultan of Egypt</note> in exchange for a compensation. Al-Nasir sent a governor and an army to the city, but later Sultan Badr al-Din seized control of it and built his royal residence there, establishing his rule. I met this Sultan outside the city as he was returning from a hunt. I dismounted from my beast for him, so he dismounted from his beast and greeted me. He welcomed me warmly. It is the custom of the kings of these lands that if a traveler dismounts for them, they are pleased by his action and increase their honor toward him; however, if he greets them while remaining mounted, they take offense and are displeased, which often leads to the traveler being deprived of their favor. This happened to me with one of them, and I regretted it. When I greeted him and remounted, he asked about my circumstances and my arrival. I entered the city with him, and he ordered that I be given the finest lodging. He used to send abundant food, fruit, and sweets in silver bowls, along with candles and robes of honor. He provided me with a mount and treated me excellently. Our stay with him was not long, and we departed for the city of Aqsaray <note>pronounced with a short 'a' on the Alif, a silent Qaf, and a short 'a' on the Sad and Ra</note>.

It is one of the most beautiful and well-constructed cities of the land of the <term>Rum</term> <gloss>Anatolia</gloss>. It is surrounded by flowing springs and orchards on every side. Three rivers flow through the city, and water runs through the houses. It contains many trees and grapevines, and there are many gardens within its walls. The famous carpets named after the city are manufactured there from sheep's wool; they have no equal in any other land. From there, they are exported to Syria, Egypt, Iraq, India, China, and the lands of the Turks. This city is under the authority of the King of Iraq <note>the Ilkhanid Mongol ruler</note>. I stayed there at the <term>zawiya</term> <gloss>hospice</gloss> of Sharif Husayn, the deputy there for Emir Arta. Arta is the deputy of the King of Iraq over the lands of the <term>Rum</term> that he has conquered. This Sharif is one of the <term>Fityan</term> <gloss>members of the youth brotherhoods</gloss> and has a large following. He showed us complete hospitality and performed the same noble deeds as those before him.

Then we traveled to the city of Niğde <note>pronounced with a short 'a' on the Nun, a silent Kaf, and a short 'a' on the Dal</note>. It is one of the cities belonging to the King of Iraq. It is a heavily populated city, though some parts of it are in ruins. It is bisected by the river known as the Black River, which is one of the great rivers. It has three bridges, one inside the city and two outside. There are waterwheels both inside and outside the city that irrigate the orchards. Fruits there are plentiful. We have set the distance from the <term>nisf al-nahar</term> <gloss>midday/meridian</gloss> because the <term>ta'dil</term> <gloss>adjustment or equation</gloss> for the birth <note>referring to the calculation of the new moon or the beginning of a cycle</note> is easier by this method than by working with the horizons. The hours of the longest day for the latitude of <term>Bayt al-Maqdis</term> <gloss>Jerusalem</gloss> are fourteen hours and a fraction. The Jewish method of calculation using <term>al-sa'at al-zamaniyya</term> <gloss>seasonal or temporal hours</gloss> is only correct if the <term>ijtima'</term> <gloss>conjunction</gloss> for the beginning of <term>Tishrei</term> <gloss>the first month of the Hebrew calendar</gloss> occurs exactly at the autumnal equinox. However, it never occurs exactly with it; rather, it precedes or follows it by a considerable amount, as we have explained previously.

When we extract the time of conjunction using the calculation provided by the Jews in the table which we have analyzed according to their opinion, we proceed from that to the knowledge of the first day of the year and the determination of its quality: whether it is <term>naqisan</term> <gloss>deficient</gloss>, <term>mu'tadilan</term> <gloss>regular</gloss>, or <term>tamman</term> <gloss>complete</gloss>. We already possess the knowledge of whether the year is <term>basita</term> <gloss>common/plain</gloss> or <term>kabisa</term> <gloss>leap/intercalary</gloss>. We then search in the Table of Limits for a duration of the days of the week whose two boundaries encompass the time we calculated for the conjunction. We look in the section for leap years if it is a leap year, and in the section for common years if it is a common year. When we find it, we find alongside it the first day of the week for the start of the year and its specific quality. Once we know the start of the year and its quality, and combine that quality with its status as common or leap, we can determine the beginning of the following year.

I am the worldly one as well. Just as I am the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> <gloss>Complete Enjoyment Body</gloss>, which is the natural result of the <term>Dharmakaya</term> <gloss>Truth Body</gloss> of Great Bliss, so too am I the world that has become the natural result of the Great Bliss of the father, the mother, and the sentient beings of the intermediate state. I am also the <term>gandharva</term> <gloss>scent-eater/intermediate state being</gloss> who is swooning with Great Bliss.

If one asks: "How is that which is the Great Bliss of the worldly ones the primary object of meditation?" It is said: "That which is called <term>Sahajananda</term> <gloss>Co-emergent Joy</gloss>," and so forth. 

Then, if one asks: "If you are the primary Great Bliss that is to be accomplished, and the co-emergent pleasure of <term>Samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of existence</gloss> is not the object of accomplishment, why are you the primary object of accomplishment?" It is said: "If it is so, then I..." and so forth. The word "also" carries the meaning of "cause," because it establishes confidence in that very essence as the primary. Because the realization is established through a corresponding example, that very essence is designated as "I, the primary."

"Like a lamp in the darkness." This means that just as a lamp makes a pot or other objects in a dark room clearly understood, the Co-emergent Joy of the example makes the Great Bliss that is to be accomplished clear.

To clarify the meaning of the words "I dwell in <term>Sukhavati</term> <gloss>The Blissful Pure Land</gloss>," and so forth, it is said: "The teacher of the thirty..." and so forth. The primary is the <term>Sambhogakaya</term> who enjoys the <term>Dharma</term> together with the <term>Bodhisattvas</term> <gloss>awakening beings</gloss> born in that body blazing with the major and minor marks of a Buddha. It means: "A self such as this resides in the Land of Bliss."

The "Consort" refers to the <term>Vajra</term> Consort <note>the wisdom consort in the context of the completion stage</note> and the consort of the example <note>the physical consort used in practice</note>. I reside in their <term>bhaga</term> <gloss>source of phenomena/womb</gloss> in the form of the "fluid." The "fluid" refers to the seed of <term>Jnana</term> <gloss>pristine wisdom</gloss> and the external seed of the example. "That" is called the fluid. 

Therefore, Great Bliss is that which depends upon the seed and the perfect union of body and speech. Without that, since it cannot arise from any other cause, one must generate bliss from the body of the deity's union. Consequently, those who seek the Great Bliss that is to be accomplished must certainly meditate on the <term>Devata Yoga</term> <gloss>Deity Yoga</gloss>. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the statement, "I do not perceive any phenomenon that attains perfect enlightenment, nor any phenomenon through which one attains perfect enlightenment," this means that although I understand all phenomena in every aspect through conventional knowledge subsumed under the wisdom of omniscience, when analyzed through ultimate wisdom, no phenomenon is seen as either a knower or an object to be known, just like objects seen in a dream.

The phrase, "O sons of the gods, it is because all phenomena are utterly pure," means that in this context, "purity" refers to the very absence of any entity. It is a synonym for "utterly non-existent."

The statement, "Blessed One, it is not difficult to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment," is made because all phenomena are non-existent. It is not difficult to realize that a non-entity is indeed a non-entity. It would be difficult to realize the true nature of phenomena if they were existent things. It is not difficult to know and practice the realization that what is non-existent is merely a non-entity. For if phenomena were existent, one would need to practice the perfections and other conducts to increase virtuous qualities and abandon non-virtuous qualities. However, because these phenomena do not exist, the practice is not difficult. Therefore, it is said that "attaining perfect enlightenment is not difficult."

The intention behind the Elder Shariputra's statement that attaining perfect enlightenment is difficult is as follows: If it were enough to simply remain in silence after realizing that all phenomena are of the nature of non-entities, void like space, then it would not be difficult. However, one must realize that in truth there is no attainment of perfect enlightenment for any phenomenon, and yet, following that realization, one must still engage in the practices of the perfections and perfectly realize all phenomena.

# The Explanation of the Noble Four Dharmas

Homage to Manjushri, the youthful.

Why was this <term>sutra</term> <gloss>scriptural discourse</gloss> composed, which states: "A <term>bodhisattva mahasattva</term> <gloss>great heroic being of awakening</gloss> should not abandon these four <term>dharmas</term> <gloss>qualities or teachings</gloss> for as long as they live, even for the sake of their life"?

It was composed to correctly show the methods for attaining unsurpassed awakening to those who are confused about entering the Great Vehicle <note>Mahayana</note>. It is to cause the heedless to correctly adopt the practice, to uplift those who are discouraged, and to bring joy to those who have correctly entered the path.

The number "four" is mentioned to prevent the rejection of the teachings by those who might fear they are too extensive. By stating the number, they are easily remembered. Furthermore, the qualities of patience and gentleness, which appear below, are not differentiated because they serve a single purpose.

Although there are many categories of those who have correctly entered the Great Vehicle, two names <note>Bodhisattva and Mahasattva</note> are mentioned for three reasons: interest, application, and realization.

How is it by interest? One is a <term>bodhisattva</term> <gloss>awakening being</gloss> because of interest in the profound objects of knowledge. One is a <term>mahasattva</term> <gloss>great being</gloss> because of interest in great power.

How is it by application? It is because one strives for the sake of one's own unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and for the sake of fully protecting all sentient beings from suffering.

How is it by realization? It is because awakening is realized through two strengths. What are the two? The strength of intelligence and the strength of diligence. One cannot realize awakening through ignorance or through small diligence.

### ON ALCHEMY

<margin>The end of Alchemy is not gold and silver, but secrets.</margin>
<margin>Poison even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that poison lies hidden and exists even in the best things? Everyone is compelled to confess this. If this is true, I now ask you whether the poison should not be separated from the good and useful? And the good accepted, the evil left behind? Indeed, it must be so. If, therefore, it is necessary, I pray you, tell me how it is separated in your workshops? For among you, everything remains mixed together. But so that you may protect your simplicity, if you are convicted into confessing that poison lies hidden there and are asked where it finally goes, then you bring forth I know not what concerning "corrections" which are supposed to drive out and take away the poison, <margin>The correction of Physicians is examined.</margin> just as they say Quince corrects <term>Scammony</term> <gloss>a harsh purgative resin</gloss>, and later <term>Diagridium</term> <gloss>purified scammony</gloss>. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterward just as it was at first? And yet you meanwhile boast that you have corrected it, so much so that the poison no longer harms. But where did it escape to? <margin>Diagridion.</margin> It remains in the Diagridium. Try it, if you are wise: exceed the limit, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know it quite quickly. Thus you also correct <term>Turbith</term> <gloss>an Ayurvedic purgative root</gloss>, and you call it <term>Diaturbith</term>. Such are your corrections, which would be fit for peasants and should be given to pack-horses. Make the danger by exceeding the limit and increase the dose: you will see if you do not feel the poison. <margin>What it is to correct a Medicine.</margin> *To correct is to take what has been corrected.* He who is malicious and has sinned: if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of him who was punished lasts. Such are these corrections also; the power lies with the substances themselves, not with you. Now, in this case, a Physician must consider nothing further than that the poison be removed. This must be done through separation. As, for example: a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted for food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it with no harm. The same must be understood equally concerning all other things, namely that there is need for a similar separation. Until that is done, you cannot be secure in your operation, unless by chance it happens that nature supplies your deficiencies, or a greater benevolence of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection will have remained.

Now, therefore, at last, if that true foundation which takes away poison is required, let us see how Alchemy provides it. For it is necessary that it be done in such a way that, if Mars is in the Sun, Mars is removed; and if Saturn is in Venus, he is separated from her. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies also exist in them. But as for those bodies which are contrary, it is altogether necessary that some of them be removed and taken away, so that in this way all contrariety is abolished, and the evil is removed from the good which you seek. <margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin> Just as gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire, so a Medicine is much less useful which does not pass through the fire. ## CHAPTER II.

There is, therefore, in all metals a true Mercury and a right sulfur, equally in the imperfect as in the perfect metals. It has merely been contaminated and made impure in the imperfect metals, which alone are deprived of perfect maturation. For these same reasons, they can be reduced to gold and silver; that is, so that the impurity with which they had been defiled may be separated from the golden or silver nature that is within them, and the form of gold or silver may be introduced into them. For they were torn away from Nature because they were removed and dug out from their natural passages, mines, and veins of the earth. Therefore, they can no longer have any operation within themselves as if they were still hiding under the earth; nevertheless, as much as is in them, they desire to be perfected.
